title: Multimodal Systems
description: Explore AI systems that process and generate text, images, audio, video, and structured signals. Learn multimodal representations, modality encoders, cross-attention, fusion architectures, contrastive learning, alignment, evaluation, and practical system design.
learningObjectives: Define multimodal learning and distinguish early, intermediate, and late fusion.
Explain how different modalities are converted into model-compatible representations.
Understand joint embedding spaces and contrastive learning.
Describe cross-attention and its role in connecting information across modalities.
Explain image patch embeddings, audio tokenization, and video frame sampling.
Understand alignment between text, images, speech, and other signals.
Design a multimodal processing pipeline with validation and provenance.
Evaluate multimodal systems using task-specific metrics and human assessment.
Identify limitations involving hallucinations, bias, privacy, temporal reasoning, and robustness.
Build a conceptual image-question-answering and multimodal retrieval prototype.

sections.title: What Are Multimodal Systems?
sections.content: A multimodal system processes, relates, or generates information from more than one modality. Common modalities include text, images, audio, video, and structured sensor signals. A text-only model may answer questions from written descriptions, while a multimodal model can potentially answer questions about an image, interpret speech, summarize a video, or connect a chart with an explanation. Multimodality is not simply the ability to accept several file formats. The model must represent information from different sources and use their relationships to perform a task. Systems vary widely: some use separate specialized models connected by application logic, while others learn shared representations or combine modalities inside one neural architecture.

sections.title: Why Combine Modalities?
sections.content: Different modalities provide complementary evidence. An image can show the physical layout of a scene, text can explain the user's goal, and audio can convey speech or environmental sounds. Combining them can reduce ambiguity and enable tasks that a single modality cannot perform reliably. For example, answering a question about a graph may require reading its visual structure and understanding the natural-language question. However, combining modalities also introduces alignment problems, more expensive computation, additional failure modes, and greater privacy risks. The best system uses only the modalities that materially improve the task.

sections.title: Common Modalities and Their Properties
sections.content: Text is a discrete sequence of tokens with linguistic structure. Images are spatial arrays of pixel values and often contain objects, text, textures, and relationships. Audio is a time-varying signal containing speech, music, environmental sounds, and silence. Video is a temporal sequence of frames, often accompanied by audio. Structured sensor data may contain time series, coordinates, or measurements. These representations differ in dimensionality, temporal structure, noise, and semantic density. A multimodal architecture must account for those differences rather than assuming that every input can be processed identically.

sections.title: A General Multimodal Pipeline
sections.content: A typical pipeline validates the input, decodes the media, preprocesses each modality, creates modality-specific representations, aligns or fuses those representations, performs the requested task, and validates the output. Image preprocessing may resize and normalize pixels. Audio preprocessing may resample a waveform or compute a spectrogram. Video processing may sample frames and preserve timestamps. The model then combines the resulting features using an architecture suited to the task. The final stage produces text, a label, a generated signal, or another structured result. Production systems should preserve source metadata and avoid discarding timestamps or modality provenance when those details affect correctness.

sections.title: Representations Across Modalities
sections.content: Neural networks usually operate on numeric tensors rather than raw human concepts. Each modality therefore needs a representation. Text is commonly converted into token IDs and learned token embeddings. Images may be represented using convolutional feature maps or patch embeddings. Audio can be represented using waveform samples, spectral features, or learned audio tokens. Video can be represented as frame features, spatiotemporal patches, or sequences of encoded events. Modality encoders map these inputs into feature spaces where useful patterns can be learned. The representations may remain separate or be projected into a shared space.

sections.title: Image Patches and Visual Tokens
sections.content: One common approach divides an image into fixed-size patches. Each patch is flattened or otherwise encoded and projected into a vector. Positional information is added so the model can distinguish where each patch originated. A Transformer then processes the sequence of visual tokens. If an image has height H and width W and non-overlapping square patches of size P are used, the number of patches is approximately (H/P) times (W/P), assuming the dimensions are divisible by P. Higher image resolution usually increases the number of tokens and computation. Some systems use multiple crops or variable-resolution processing to preserve small details.

sections.title: Counting Image Patches
sections.content: For an image with dimensions H by W and square patches of side P, assuming H and W are divisible by P, the number of patches is N = (H/P)(W/P). This count excludes any additional special tokens or global representations. Doubling both image dimensions while keeping patch size fixed increases the number of patches by a factor of four.
sections.example: A 224 by 224 image divided into 16 by 16 patches produces 14 by 14 = 196 visual patches. A 448 by 448 image with the same patch size produces 28 by 28 = 784 patches.

sections.title: Resolution, Detail, and Compute
sections.content: Small text, thin lines, and fine-grained objects can disappear when an image is resized too aggressively. Increasing resolution may preserve detail, but it also increases memory use and model computation. If a Transformer processes N tokens with full self-attention, the attention matrix has quadratic dependence on N. Image-processing systems therefore balance resolution, cropping, token count, latency, and accuracy. A document-reading application may need high-resolution crops around text, while a broad scene-classification task may work well at lower resolution.

sections.title: Representing Audio
sections.content: Audio can be represented as a waveform, a time-frequency spectrogram, learned audio tokens, or text produced by speech recognition. A waveform contains sampled amplitude values over time. Spectrograms represent how energy varies across time and frequency. Speech-recognition systems may map acoustic features into text tokens, while audio-understanding systems may retain information that transcription loses, such as speaker characteristics, music, or environmental sounds. The appropriate representation depends on whether the task requires exact words, general sound understanding, timing, or audio generation.

sections.title: Sampling and Time Resolution
sections.content: A digital audio signal sampled at frequency f_s contains approximately f_s times T samples over duration T seconds, excluding endpoint conventions. Higher sampling rates preserve more high-frequency information but increase the number of samples. If a waveform contains 16,000 samples per second, a 10-second recording contains approximately 160,000 samples in one channel.
sections.formula: Number of samples approximately equals f_s * T
sections.example: For a 10-second mono recording at 16 kHz, the raw signal contains about 160,000 samples. A stereo recording has two channels and therefore approximately twice as many scalar samples.

sections.title: Video as a Temporal Sequence
sections.content: Video contains both spatial information within frames and temporal information across frames. A model that examines only one frame may recognize objects but miss motion, changes in state, or event order. Video pipelines often sample frames at fixed intervals or use event-aware sampling. Audio may be processed alongside the frames. Timestamps matter because they establish when an event occurred and allow the system to align visual evidence with spoken words. Dense frame processing can be expensive, so the system should choose a sampling strategy based on the temporal precision required by the task.

sections.title: Video Sampling Tradeoffs
sections.content: If a video lasts T seconds and frames are sampled at r frames per second, the approximate number of sampled frames is N = T*r. If each sampled frame produces K visual tokens, the visual token count is approximately T*r*K before additional temporal or special tokens. Increasing frame rate improves temporal coverage but increases compute and context usage.
sections.formula: N_frames approximately equals T * r; N_visual_tokens approximately equals T * r * K
sections.example: Sampling a 60-second video at one frame per second yields approximately 60 frames. Sampling at four frames per second yields approximately 240 frames, potentially providing better event coverage at a substantially higher processing cost.

sections.title: Early, Intermediate, and Late Fusion
sections.content: Early fusion combines representations near the input stage, allowing the model to learn relationships across modalities from the beginning. Intermediate fusion processes modalities with specialized encoders and combines their features in one or more later layers. Late fusion combines separate predictions or representations near the output stage. Early fusion can model detailed cross-modal interactions but may require substantial training data and careful handling of different input rates. Late fusion is often easier to build from existing models but may lose fine-grained interactions. Intermediate fusion offers a flexible compromise.

sections.title: Choosing a Fusion Strategy
sections.content: Consider a system that answers questions about product photographs and accompanying descriptions. Late fusion might independently classify the image and process the text, then combine their predictions. Intermediate fusion could encode the image and text separately and let cross-attention connect the representations. Early fusion could combine low-level or token-level representations before much task-specific processing. If the task requires grounding a particular phrase in a particular image region, an architecture with explicit cross-modal interaction is generally more suitable than simply averaging independent predictions.

sections.title: Joint Embedding Spaces
sections.content: A joint embedding space maps different modalities into a representation space where semantically related examples are close. For example, a text encoder may represent the phrase 'a red bicycle' while an image encoder represents a photograph of a red bicycle. If training aligns these vectors, the system can retrieve images using text or retrieve descriptions using images. The encoders do not need identical internal architectures, but their output vectors must be compatible under the learned similarity measure. Joint embedding spaces support cross-modal retrieval, clustering, zero-shot classification, and semantic search.

sections.title: Similarity Between Modalities
sections.content: A common similarity measure is cosine similarity. It compares the angle between two vectors and is insensitive to their magnitudes when both vectors are nonzero. Higher cosine similarity can indicate stronger semantic alignment when the representation space has been trained for that purpose. Similarity scores should not automatically be interpreted as probabilities.
sections.example: Suppose a text embedding and an image embedding have cosine similarity 0.87. This suggests strong alignment relative to many lower-scoring candidates in the same representation space, but the value alone does not guarantee that the image exactly matches the description.

sections.title: Contrastive Learning
sections.content: Contrastive learning trains a representation model to bring related examples closer and push unrelated examples apart under a chosen similarity measure. In image-text learning, a batch may contain matched image-caption pairs. The training objective encourages each image to align with its correct caption more strongly than with other captions in the batch. This supports retrieval and transfer to tasks not explicitly labeled during pretraining. The quality of the learned space depends on data quality, negative examples, batch construction, and the diversity of concepts represented.

sections.title: A Contrastive Objective
sections.content: A common contrastive objective computes similarities between image and text embeddings, scales them by a temperature parameter, and applies a cross-entropy loss so that matched pairs receive high relative scores. Training often uses both image-to-text and text-to-image directions. The exact formulation varies by model and implementation.
sections.example: Here B is the batch size, s(i,j) is the similarity between image i and text j, and tau is a positive temperature. The denominator includes competing captions. The model is rewarded when the correct caption receives a higher similarity than alternatives.

sections.title: Cross-Attention Between Modalities
sections.content: Cross-attention allows a representation from one modality to select relevant information from another. For example, text tokens representing the question 'What color is the car?' can attend to visual tokens corresponding to the car. In standard cross-attention, queries come from one sequence while keys and values come from another. This creates a learned information exchange rather than requiring the model to compress both modalities into one vector before interaction. Cross-attention is useful for visual question answering, grounded captioning, speech-text alignment, and multimodal generation.

sections.title: Cross-Attention Mathematics
sections.content: Let Q represent queries from one modality and K and V represent keys and values from another modality. Attention computes compatibility scores between queries and keys, normalizes them, and uses the resulting weights to combine values. The output depends on the query modality and the information available in the key-value modality.
sections.formula: CrossAttention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
sections.example: In visual question answering, Q may come from encoded question tokens while K and V come from image patches. Each question token can then gather information from the visual patches most relevant to its meaning.

sections.title: Cross-Modal Alignment
sections.content: Alignment concerns which parts of different modalities correspond to one another. A spoken phrase may align with a word sequence, an object label may align with a bounding box, and a video event may align with a timestamp. Alignment can be global, such as matching an entire image with a caption, or local, such as associating a phrase with a region. Global alignment is useful for retrieval but may not preserve exact object-level relationships. Local alignment is important for grounding, temporal reasoning, and fine-grained verification.

sections.title: Multimodal Input and Output
sections.content: A multimodal system may accept several input modalities and produce one output modality, or it may generate multiple types of output. Image question answering accepts an image and text and returns text. Text-to-speech accepts text and generates audio. Text-to-image systems produce images from textual descriptions. Real-time voice assistants may combine audio perception, language understanding, tool execution, and audio generation. Input and output capabilities should be distinguished explicitly because a model that understands images does not necessarily generate images, and a speech recognizer does not necessarily generate natural speech.

sections.title: Autoregressive Multimodal Generation
sections.content: Autoregressive models generate a sequence by repeatedly predicting the next token conditioned on preceding tokens. In multimodal systems, the sequence may contain text tokens, image-related tokens, audio tokens, or modality markers. The model can learn dependencies across modalities when the training objective and data represent those dependencies. Some systems instead use separate encoders and decoders or diffusion-based components for particular modalities. There is no single architecture that describes all modern multimodal models.

sections.title: Speech Recognition and Speech Generation
sections.content: Speech systems may perform automatic speech recognition, speech translation, speaker diarization, speech synthesis, or conversational audio interaction. Recognition maps an audio signal to words. Translation maps speech in one language to text or speech in another. Diarization identifies which speaker spoke when. Synthesis generates speech from text or another conditioning signal. A pipeline may use separate models for these stages or an integrated model. Timing, accents, noise, overlapping speech, language coverage, and speaker privacy are important practical considerations.

sections.title: Document and Chart Understanding
sections.content: Documents combine visual layout and linguistic content. Reading a document may require detecting text, understanding columns, connecting labels to values, recognizing tables, and interpreting diagrams. Charts add a further challenge: the model must connect axes, scales, legends, colors, and plotted data. Flattening a page into plain text can lose spatial relationships. A robust document pipeline may combine OCR, layout detection, visual reasoning, table extraction, and language-model interpretation. Critical numerical claims should be verified against extracted values or the original document.

sections.title: Computing Embedding Similarity
sections.content:
import numpy as np

def cosine_similarity(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> float:
    a = np.asarray(a, dtype=np.float64)
    b = np.asarray(b, dtype=np.float64)
    if a.shape != b.shape:
        raise ValueError("Embeddings must have the same shape")
    norm_a = np.linalg.norm(a)
    norm_b = np.linalg.norm(b)
    if norm_a == 0 or norm_b == 0:
        raise ValueError("Zero vectors do not have a defined cosine similarity")
    return float(np.dot(a, b) / (norm_a * norm_b))

text_embedding = np.array([0.8, 0.2, 0.5])
image_embedding = np.array([0.7, 0.3, 0.6])
print(cosine_similarity(text_embedding, image_embedding))
sections.explanation: The example illustrates the mathematics of similarity using mock vectors. Real cross-modal retrieval requires encoders trained to place the modalities into a compatible embedding space. Arbitrary image and text embeddings cannot be meaningfully compared just because they have the same dimensionality.

sections.title: Multimodal Retrieval Systems
sections.content: Multimodal retrieval allows a query in one modality to retrieve relevant items represented in another. A text query can retrieve images, an image can retrieve similar images, and a spoken request can retrieve documents after speech recognition or direct audio encoding. A typical architecture encodes corpus items, stores their vectors and metadata, encodes the query, retrieves nearest candidates, and optionally reranks the results. The system should preserve permissions and source metadata during retrieval. Similarity is a ranking signal, not proof of factual correspondence.

sections.title: A Cross-Modal Search Pipeline
sections.content: For text-to-image retrieval, first decode and validate the images. Generate embeddings using a compatible image encoder and store the vectors with image identifiers, access-control metadata, and source information. When a query arrives, encode it using the corresponding text encoder and retrieve nearest vectors using the trained similarity measure. Apply permission filters before returning results. If needed, rerank the candidates using a more detailed relevance model. Return images with provenance and make clear when the ranking reflects similarity rather than verified identity or exact matching.

sections.title: Basic Image Preprocessing
sections.content:
from PIL import Image

def inspect_image(path: str) -> dict:
    with Image.open(path) as image:
        return {
            "format": image.format,
            "mode": image.mode,
            "width": image.width,
            "height": image.height
        }

metadata = inspect_image("example.jpg")
print(metadata)
sections.explanation: This small example inspects image metadata. A production pipeline should enforce file-size and dimension limits, allow only supported formats, handle corrupted files, and apply appropriate decoding and normalization before inference.

sections.title: Audio Preprocessing Considerations
sections.content: Audio preprocessing may include resampling, channel conversion, clipping detection, silence handling, normalization, and segmentation. The target sample rate must match the model's expected input. Downmixing stereo audio can simplify processing but may remove useful spatial information. Segmenting a long recording can reduce memory usage, but segment boundaries can split words or events. If exact transcription is required, preserve timestamps and avoid discarding low-confidence segments. Record the preprocessing configuration so that results can be reproduced.

sections.title: Latency and Computational Cost
sections.content: Multimodal inference can require more preprocessing, larger context windows, multiple encoders, and additional model stages. Latency depends on media size, resolution, duration, token count, batching, hardware, and model architecture. A voice interaction may be sensitive to delay, while offline video summarization may tolerate longer processing. Optimize the actual task rather than minimizing every component independently. Caching reusable embeddings, limiting unnecessary frames, batching compatible inputs, and selecting an appropriate model can improve efficiency without sacrificing essential information.

sections.title: Attention Cost Across Modalities
sections.content: For full self-attention over N tokens, the attention score matrix contains N squared pairwise scores per attention head. This makes long visual or audio sequences expensive. The exact total compute depends on model width, layers, implementation, and hardware, but the quadratic relationship explains why increasing the number of tokens can substantially increase cost.
sections.formula: Number of attention score entries per head = N^2
sections.example: Increasing a sequence from 1,000 to 2,000 tokens increases the number of pairwise attention score entries from 1,000,000 to 4,000,000. Efficient attention variants, local attention, pooling, or token reduction can reduce practical costs.

sections.title: Evaluating Multimodal Systems
sections.content: Evaluation must match the task. Image classification may use accuracy and per-class recall. Text-image retrieval may use recall at k, mean reciprocal rank, or normalized discounted cumulative gain. Speech recognition may use word error rate. Object detection may use intersection over union and average precision. Captioning and open-ended question answering may require human judgments of correctness, relevance, grounding, and completeness. Video understanding may require temporal accuracy. Evaluate performance across lighting, accents, camera quality, language, demographic groups, and unusual inputs rather than reporting only an aggregate score.

sections.title: Grounding and Hallucination
sections.content: A multimodal model can produce a fluent answer that is not supported by the supplied image, audio, or video. It may invent objects, misread small text, infer an event that is not visible, or confuse two similar entities. Grounding means connecting a claim to evidence in the input. Systems can improve grounding by preserving relevant crops, extracting OCR text, retrieving supporting frames, attaching timestamps, and asking for evidence-aware outputs. High-impact conclusions should be verified using independent measurements or human review. A plausible answer is not equivalent to an observed fact.

sections.title: Robustness to Noise and Distribution Shift
sections.content: Real-world media differs from training data. Images may be blurry, rotated, dark, compressed, or partially obscured. Audio may contain noise, accents, reverberation, or overlapping speakers. Videos may have unusual frame rates or abrupt scene changes. A model may also encounter unfamiliar objects, languages, layouts, or cultural contexts. Evaluate robustness using controlled perturbations and representative field data. Detect unsupported input conditions where possible, communicate uncertainty, and provide fallback behavior rather than forcing a confident answer for every input.

sections.title: Bias and Representation
sections.content: Multimodal models inherit biases from their training data, annotation practices, and evaluation benchmarks. A system may associate visual appearance with stereotyped occupations, perform unevenly across skin tones, misunderstand dialects, or underperform on underrepresented languages. Bias can arise from the interaction of modalities as well as from individual encoders. Evaluate relevant subgroups and task-specific error patterns, document known limitations, and avoid using unsupported demographic inference for consequential decisions.

sections.title: Privacy and Sensitive Media
sections.content: Images, audio, and video can reveal faces, locations, documents, private conversations, and other sensitive information. Before processing media, determine whether the system has a valid basis for collecting and using it. Limit retention, restrict access, protect stored files, and avoid placing raw media in ordinary logs. Remove unnecessary metadata where appropriate and be cautious with location information embedded in files. Consent, retention, deletion, and access requirements should be designed into the pipeline rather than added after deployment.

sections.title: Security Risks in Multimodal Inputs
sections.content: Multimodal inputs can contain adversarial or misleading content. An image may contain text intended to manipulate a model, an audio clip may contain hidden or spoken instructions, and a video may alternate benign and malicious frames. These inputs should not be allowed to override application policy. If a multimodal model can call tools, apply the same strict authorization and execution boundaries used in text-only systems. Validate media files, enforce resource limits, sandbox decoders where appropriate, and treat extracted text and model-generated interpretations as untrusted input.

sections.title: Human Review and High-Impact Decisions
sections.content: Human review is especially important when multimodal errors could cause physical, financial, legal, or medical harm. The system should present the evidence used for a decision, preserve relevant timestamps or image regions, and communicate uncertainty. Reviewers need enough context to challenge the model rather than merely approve its output. A human approval step should not be treated as effective if the interface hides uncertainty, overwhelms reviewers with requests, or makes it difficult to inspect the original evidence.

sections.title: Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
sections.content: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation retrieves evidence from text, images, audio transcripts, video frames, or mixed documents before generating a response. A corpus may store text chunks and image embeddings separately while linking them through document identifiers and timestamps. Retrieval can combine keyword search, vector similarity, metadata filters, and reranking. The generation stage should cite or identify the retrieved evidence when the application requires traceability. Retrieval quality and generation quality should be evaluated independently because a good generator cannot reliably compensate for missing evidence.

sections.title: Designing a Multimodal Application
sections.content: Start by defining the user task and the evidence required to complete it. Select the minimum necessary modalities and decide whether to use one integrated model or a pipeline of specialized components. Specify input limits, preprocessing, representation storage, permissions, latency requirements, and fallback behavior. Define the output contract and evidence requirements. Build an evaluation set that includes common cases and realistic failures. Finally, instrument each stage so errors can be traced to media decoding, encoding, retrieval, fusion, generation, or post-processing. This modular approach makes debugging and model replacement easier.

sections.title: Mini Project: Image Question Answering and Retrieval
sections.content: Build a prototype that accepts a set of images and a natural-language question. Validate the uploaded files, generate image embeddings with a compatible pretrained encoder, and store the embeddings with identifiers and access metadata. Encode the user's question using the matching text encoder and retrieve relevant images. Use a suitable vision-language model or a clearly separated interpretation stage to answer questions about the retrieved evidence. Return the image identifiers used to form the answer. Evaluate retrieval recall, answer correctness, unsupported claims, latency, and failure behavior. Include tests for unreadable images, unrelated queries, ambiguous questions, and malicious text embedded in an image.

sections.title: Further Research Directions
sections.content: Important research directions include high-resolution vision, efficient video understanding, real-time speech interaction, spatial reasoning, multimodal retrieval, temporal alignment, unified token spaces, grounded generation, and data-efficient adaptation. Other active concerns include reducing hallucinations, improving robustness under distribution shift, supporting lower-resource languages, and measuring fairness across real-world populations. Compare approaches using task-specific evidence and reproducible evaluation rather than assuming that a larger or more unified model is automatically better.

exercises.question: What makes an AI system multimodal?
exercises.correctAnswer: It processes, relates, or generates information across more than one modality, such as text, images, audio, or video.
exercises.solution: Multimodality requires more than accepting different file types. The system must represent or combine information from multiple modalities for a task.

exercises.question: What is the difference between early fusion and late fusion?
exercises.correctAnswer: Early fusion combines modality representations near the input stage, while late fusion combines separate outputs or representations near the end.
exercises.solution: Early fusion enables detailed interactions but can be more complex. Late fusion is modular but may lose fine-grained cross-modal relationships.

exercises.question: How many non-overlapping 16 by 16 patches are produced by a 224 by 224 image?
Approximately how many samples are in a 5-second mono audio recording sampled at 16 kHz?
exercises.solution: Samples approximately equal sample rate multiplied by duration: 16,000 * 5 = 80,000.

exercises.question: A video is 30 seconds long and sampled at two frames per second. Approximately how many frames are processed?
exercises.solution: The frame count is approximately duration multiplied by sampling rate: 30 * 2 = 60.

exercises.question: Why are aligned image and text embeddings useful?
exercises.correctAnswer: They allow semantically related images and text to be compared or retrieved using a shared similarity measure.
exercises.solution: A text query can retrieve images when the encoders have learned a compatible joint embedding space.

exercises.question: What information can be lost when a video is represented by only one frame?
exercises.correctAnswer: Motion, event order, temporal changes, and events occurring outside that frame.
exercises.solution: A single frame may represent the scene but cannot reliably capture the full temporal sequence.

exercises.question: A vision-language model confidently reports a serial number that is too small to read in the supplied image. What should a reliable system do?
exercises.correctAnswer: Avoid treating the answer as verified, inspect a higher-resolution crop or OCR result, and request human review if necessary.
exercises.solution: Fluent generation does not guarantee that the model actually observed the detail. Critical values should be grounded in inspectable evidence.

exercises.question: An image contains text instructing an AI assistant to export private records. How should a tool-enabled multimodal application respond?
exercises.correctAnswer: Treat the text as untrusted image content and enforce the normal tool allowlist, authorization, and approval requirements.
exercises.solution: Instructions embedded in media must not override application policy or grant access to privileged operations.

exercises.question: Design a high-level system for searching a photo collection using text queries.
exercises.correctAnswer: Validate images, encode them with an image encoder, store vectors and metadata, encode queries with a compatible text encoder, retrieve nearest candidates, enforce access filters, and return ranked results.
exercises.solution: The text and image encoders must produce compatible embeddings. Evaluation should measure retrieval quality, latency, permission correctness, and robustness to ambiguous queries.

exercises.question: Why does increasing the number of Transformer tokens from 1,000 to 2,000 increase the full-attention score matrix size by four times?
exercises.correctAnswer: The number of pairwise attention scores scales quadratically with the sequence length.
exercises.solution: The score count changes from 1,000 squared, or 1,000,000, to 2,000 squared, or 4,000,000.

exercises.question: How should a multimodal system be evaluated if it answers questions about videos?
exercises.correctAnswer: Measure answer correctness and grounding, temporal accuracy, robustness, latency, and performance across representative video conditions.
exercises.solution: A system can identify objects correctly but misunderstand the order of events. Evaluation should include the spatial and temporal requirements of the task.

summary: Multimodal systems connect information from text, images, audio, video, and other signals using modality-specific encoders, shared embedding spaces, cross-attention, fusion architectures, and specialized generation components. Their capabilities depend on representation quality, alignment, input resolution, temporal coverage, and computational constraints. Reliable applications combine task-specific preprocessing with grounding, evaluation, privacy controls, security boundaries, and human review where the consequences of error are significant.
